items.title: Top 5 Biggest Impact Craters on Earth (#2 Killed the Dinosaurs) #shorts
items.description:
From a ring-shaped lake in Canada to a 2-billion-year-old scar in South Africa, drawn to scale.
Full video: What If an Asteroid Hit the Ocean? A 10 km Rock Would Hit the Seafloor

Sources
• Earth Impact Database (Planetary and Space Science Centre, University of New Brunswick): Vredefort about 160 km, about 2.02 billion years; Chicxulub about 150 km, about 66 million years; Sudbury about 130 km, about 1.85 billion years; Popigai about 100 km, about 35.7 million years; Manicouagan about 100 km, about 214 million years (some sources give other sizes, measured as the eroded or the original crater)
• UNESCO World Heritage: Vredefort Dome, the oldest and largest impact structure found on Earth
• NASA: the Chicxulub impactor was about 10 km wide and struck about 66 million years ago
• Popigai: impact diamonds formed from graphite by the shock of the impact (Russian Academy of Sciences)
• Own calculation: 160 km / 42.195 km (marathon) ≈ 3.8

Visuals are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.

items.title: What If an Asteroid Hit the Ocean? A 10 km Rock Would Hit the Seafloor
items.description:
71% of Earth is ocean, so most space rocks land in water. We drop five rocks into the same ocean, from an 18 m Chelyabinsk-size rock to the 10 km Chicxulub impactor, and see where the water saves us and where it makes things worse.

Chapters
0:00 A rock taller than the ocean is deep
0:15 The drop test: five rocks, one ocean
0:34 Rock 1: 18 m, the Chelyabinsk blast
1:28 Rock 2: 140 m, a crater made of water
2:38 Rock 3: 250 m, the ocean goes up as steam
3:17 Rock 4: 1 km, an ozone hole for the planet
4:00 Eltanin: the deep sea took the hit
4:22 Rock 5: 10 km, Chicxulub
4:53 The mile-high tsunami
5:51 Footprints under Louisiana
6:13 The twist: does the ocean protect us?
6:57 How we push back: DART and NEO Surveyor
7:23 Recap and next episode

Sources
• NOAA: the ocean covers about 71% of Earth's surface; average ocean depth about 3,682 m (Charette and Smith, Oceanography, 2010)
• NASA: the Chicxulub impactor was about 10 km wide and struck about 66 million years ago; crater about 150 km wide (Earth Impact Database)
• NASA: the Chelyabinsk meteor (15 February 2013) was about 18 m wide, broke up roughly 30 km up and released about 440 kilotons; about 1,500 people were injured, mostly by broken glass
• NASA Planetary Defense: about 25,000 near-Earth asteroids are 140 m or larger; roughly 40% have been found
• G. Gisler (Los Alamos National Laboratory), American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting 2016: impact waves dissipate quickly; dangerous near populated shores (about 100 km); a ~250 m impact can vaporize up to 250 megatons of water; 'the most significant effect of an impact into the ocean is the injection of water vapor into the stratosphere, with possible climate effects'
• E. Pierazzo et al., Earth and Planetary Science Letters (2010), 'Ozone perturbation from medium-size asteroid impacts in the ocean': 1 km ocean impact, more than 70% ozone loss at mid-high latitudes for over two years, UV index up to 56
• World Health Organization: UV index 11 and above is 'extreme'
• Eltanin impact: about 2.5 million years ago, Bellingshausen Sea (Southern Ocean), water 4 to 5 km deep, impactor roughly 1 km (estimates 1 to 4 km), no confirmed crater (Gersonde et al., Nature 1997)
• M. Range et al., AGU Advances (2022): Chicxulub tsunami about 1.5 km high within about 10 minutes; reached most coastlines within 48 hours; initial energy up to 30,000 times the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami; open-ocean waves over 10 m approaching North Atlantic coasts
• G. Kinsland et al., Earth and Planetary Science Letters (2021): buried megaripples in Louisiana, about 1.5 km deep, average height 16 m and spacing 600 m (interpretation debated)
• NASA/NOAA Asteroid Generated Tsunami Workshop 2016 (Morrison and Venkatapathy, NASA TM 2017): the tsunami contribution to overall impact hazard is substantially less than that of land impacts
• NASA: DART (26 September 2022) shortened Dimorphos's 11 h 55 min orbit by 32 minutes; NEO Surveyor launch no earlier than September 2027 (JPL)
• NASA CNEOS: no known asteroid larger than 1 km has a significant chance of hitting Earth in the next 100 years
• Burj Khalifa: 828 m tall; 1.5 km / 828 m ≈ 1.8
• Own calculations: 10 / 3.682 ≈ 2.7; 3.7 km at 20 km/s ≈ 0.2 s; deep-water wave speed = √(9.81 m/s² × 3,682 m) ≈ 190 m/s ≈ 684 km/h; 440 kt ≈ 30 × Hiroshima (15 kt)

—

Visuals and animations are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.

items.title: Our Entire Solar System Fits Inside This Black Hole #shorts
items.description:
38 billion km across: M87*, the first black hole ever photographed, with our solar system drawn to scale inside its event horizon.
Full video: The Speed of Light Is Slow. Here's the Proof (Even at 1 Billion km/h)

Sources
• Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019), Astrophysical Journal Letters: M87* has about 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun; first image of a black hole, released 10 April 2019
• NASA: Neptune orbits about 30.07 AU from the Sun (1 AU = 149.6 million km)
• NASA/JPL: Voyager 1 launched 5 September 1977 and reaches one light-day (about 25.9 billion km) from Earth in November 2026
• Own calculations: Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c² for 6.5 billion solar masses ≈ 19.2 billion km (128 AU), diameter ≈ 38.4 billion km; Neptune's orbit 60.1 AU across, 257 / 60.1 ≈ 4.3; light crossing 38.4 billion km / 299,792 km/s ≈ 35.6 hours; Voyager 1 at about 173 AU ≈ 1.35 times the radius (illustration with the Sun placed at the centre)

Visuals are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
#shorts #space #blackhole #science
